title: DDT drove peregrine falcons to local extinction by thinning their eggshells
body: The peregrine is famous for its hunting stoop, widely reported at over 320 km/h, though radar studies have confirmed far lower speeds. In the 1950s, 60s and 70s it crashed across much of its range, because the pesticide **DDT** built up in the birds and thinned their eggshells, so fewer eggs survived to hatch. It disappeared from parts of the south-eastern United States and from Belgium. After DDT was banned in the early 1970s, nest protection and the release of captive-bred birds brought it back: the United States removed it from its endangered list in 1999, Canada declared it no longer at risk in 2017, and peregrines now nest on cathedrals, skyscraper ledges and bridges, hunting city pigeons.

slides.question: Why did DDT make peregrine eggs fail?
slides.explanation: DDT built up in the birds' bodies and thinned their eggshells, so fewer eggs survived to hatch. Populations crashed from the 1950s to the 1970s and recovered after the bans of the early 1970s.

events.text: Endangered in Canada; one pair left in the Yukon
Taken off the US endangered list

slides.alt: A peregrine falcon perched on a steep, lichen-covered rock ledge, looking down
slides.caption: Cliff ledges are the classic nest site. In many parts of its range the peregrine now also nests on tall buildings and bridges, where feral pigeons are its main prey.

left.label: Often claimed
left.text: Over 320 km/h; a 2005 television programme reported a dive clocked at 389 km/h.

right.label: Measured
right.text: Radar tracks have never confirmed such speeds; the highest reliably measured is 184 km/h.

slides.prompt: Which large US city made the peregrine falcon its official city bird?
slides.detail: Peregrines have adapted to cities worldwide, nesting on cathedrals, skyscraper window ledges and tower blocks. The first recorded urban pair nested on Swansea Guildhall in the 1980s.

slides.label: breeding pairs in the UK in 2011, by RSPB estimate
slides.text: The UK population crashed in the 1960s and recovered after DDT was banned. British peregrines have become increasingly urban, especially in the south, where natural cliffs are scarce.
